clinicalPearls: ME/CFS is a chronic, complex, multisystem illness whose functional impact on daily functioning has been compared to that of multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and congestive heart failure.

The defining feature is persistent, unexplained fatigue causing substantial functional impairment, together with postexertional malaise (PEM) - worsening of symptoms after physical, mental, or emotional exertion that would not have been a problem before the illness.
PEM relapses last longer than a day and can persist for weeks; the relationship between a relapse and the preceding activity is often not apparent to the patient, so PEM may go unrecognized.

Common accompanying symptoms include pain, cognitive dysfunction (patient-described 'brain fog'), unrefreshing sleep, headache, sore throat, tender lymph nodes, muscle and joint aches, feverishness, and orthostatic intolerance.
There is no diagnostic test; diagnosis rests on a characteristic profile of patient-reported symptoms, requiring evaluation by an experienced clinician.

The 2015 Institute of Medicine criteria require substantial activity reduction with profound new-onset fatigue not relieved by rest, plus PEM, plus unrefreshing sleep, plus either cognitive impairment or orthostatic intolerance.
Routine laboratory tests are typically within normal limits in ME/CFS; their value lies in identifying alternative or contributing illnesses rather than confirming the diagnosis.

Roughly 10% of patients remain ill for 6 months or more after a variety of infections (e.g., Epstein-Barr virus, Ross River virus, Q fever, Ebola, SARS-CoV-1, Giardia); recovery is otherwise the rule.
Recognition of ME/CFS as a diagnosable component of Long COVID has increased clinical awareness, but patients still encounter stigma and misunderstanding from clinicians.
An estimated 80% or more of people who meet ME/CFS criteria have never been diagnosed by a health care provider.
Patients are reported to be more medication-sensitive than the general population, so any drug should begin at lower-than-usual doses and be increased slowly.
Patients may appear well during an office visit and then relapse afterward from the exertion of attending the consultation.
harrison.pathophysiology: ME/CFS is understood as a complex disorder involving alterations across multiple interrelated homeostatic systems rather than a single mechanism. A wide range of infectious agents (viral and nonviral) can trigger a postinfectious fatiguing illness resembling ME/CFS, and noninfectious stressors - toxins, physical trauma, adverse life events, and cumulative allostatic load ('wear and tear') - are also associated. Twin and family studies suggest contributions from shared environment and genetic factors. Evidence for immunologic dysfunction is inconsistent and not established in most patients; reported findings include modest antinuclear antibody elevations, reduced immunoglobulin subclasses, impaired mitogen-driven lymphocyte proliferation, decreased natural killer cell activity, altered cytokine production, and altered T-cell metabolism. A hypothesis that excess cytokines such as interleukin-1 or interferon-alpha drive the fatigue and flulike symptoms lacks compelling supporting data. Other inconsistent and nondiagnostic findings include nonspecific regional brain MRI changes, autonomic nervous system dysfunction, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis abnormalities, altered metabolism, and gut microbiome dysbiosis. Unifying multisystem models integrate infection, immune, central and autonomic nervous system, metabolic, genetic, lifestyle, and stress factors.
additionalDifferentials: Broad differential of fatigue (medical and psychiatric causes evaluated per chronic fatigue workup)
Anemia / iron deficiency or iron overload
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) and other dysautonomia
Idiopathic chronic fatigue (unexplained chronic fatigue not meeting full ME/CFS criteria)
infectionMimics: Postinfectious fatiguing illness following Epstein-Barr virus
Post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (Long COVID) with prolonged fatiguing illness
nonInfectiousMimics: Depression and other psychiatric conditions presenting with fatigue
additionalInvestigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
Renal function tests (blood urea nitrogen, glomerular filtration rate)
Liver function panel (bilirubin, ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, total protein, albumin/globulin ratio)
Iron studies to assess both deficiency and overload (serum iron, transferrin saturation, ferritin)
Mental health assessment screening for depression and anxiety
redFlags: Continued decline in function (should prompt evaluation for another illness rather than being attributed to ME/CFS)
New, worsening, or unusual symptoms warranting further workup for a new illness
Serious depression and increased suicide risk associated with social isolation and loss of hope
Severe disease leaving the patient essentially homebound
harrison.prognosis: Severity ranges from mild or moderate (retaining varying degrees of pre-illness function) to severe (essentially homebound). Most patients experience some improvement and stabilize, but a return to the prior level of function is unusual. A continued functional decline is atypical and should trigger evaluation for other illnesses. Because of social isolation and loss of hope, serious depression and an increased risk of suicide are reported, warranting active screening and referral.
pitfalls: Trivializing the illness or dismissing patients, contributing to stigma and underdiagnosis (most who meet criteria are never diagnosed).
Failing to recognize PEM because patients do not connect relapses to preceding exertion, and may appear well in clinic only to crash afterward.
Attributing a continued functional decline to ME/CFS rather than investigating an alternative diagnosis.
Standard-dose medication initiation in patients who are unusually drug-sensitive, increasing toxicity risk.
Encouraging overexertion on 'good days' that leads to the 'push and crash' cycle and negates functional gains.
Relying on laboratory tests for diagnosis - results are usually normal and serve only to exclude other conditions.
harrison.severityClassification: Severity is described clinically as mild/moderate (patients retain varying degrees of pre-illness function) versus severe (patients essentially homebound). Diagnostically, the 2015 IOM criteria require substantial activity reduction lasting more than 6 months with profound new-onset fatigue not relieved by rest, plus postexertional malaise, plus unrefreshing sleep, plus either cognitive impairment or orthostatic intolerance, with symptoms present at least half the time and of at least moderate intensity.
management: Energy management or pacing to keep activity within the individual's energy limits and avoid triggering post-exertional malaise, noting that graded exercise therapy is no longer recommended as it can worsen symptoms
Symptomatic treatment of pain with simple analgesics and neuropathic agents where indicated
Management of unrefreshing sleep with sleep-hygiene measures and cautious short-term use of sleep aids
Treat orthostatic intolerance with increased fluid and salt intake, compression garments and pharmacological measures where needed
Support for cognitive dysfunction with activity structuring and cognitive strategies, plus psychological support for coping with a chronic illness
Exclude and treat alternative causes of fatigue, such as thyroid disease and anaemia, before settling on the diagnosis
Multidisciplinary specialist input with re-evaluation for any atypical continued functional decline
